content: The World Health Organization (WHO) operational handbook on tuberculosis (TB) preventive treatment provides detailed guidance on key decision points for policy considerations, health system requirements, and areas requiring additional investment at each stage of the care cascade. It includes a set of standard indicators for monitoring and evaluating TB preventive treatment (TPT) services, along with recommended data variables to be integrated into national health management information systems (HMIS). The use of digital tools is encouraged to reduce the reporting burden on healthcare workers. The primary goal of this document is to support countries in achieving their contributions to global TPT targets. Specifically, the United Nations High-Level Meeting (UNHLM) targets aim to provide TPT to at least 30 million individuals between 2018 and 2022. Identifying Populations for Latent TB Infection (LTBI) Testing and Preventive Treatment 1. People Living with HIV (PLHIV): Adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB should receive TPT as part of comprehensive HIV care. This includes individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART), pregnant women, and those previously treated for TB, regardless of their level of immunosuppression or availability of LTBI testing. Infants under 12 months living with HIV who have been in contact with a person with TB and are unlikely to have active TB based on clinical evaluation or national guidelines should receive TPT. Children aged 12 months or older living with HIV in high TB transmission settings should be offered TPT as part of comprehensive HIV prevention and care, regardless of TB contact history. All children living with HIV who have successfully completed treatment for TB disease may also receive TPT. 2. Household Contacts (Regardless of HIV Status): Children under 5 years who are household contacts of individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB and are found not to have active TB should be given TPT, even if LTBI testing is unavailable. Children aged 5 years or older, adolescents, and adults who are household contacts of individuals with confirmed pulmonary TB may also be considered for TPT if active TB is excluded. Selected high-risk household contacts of patients with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) may be considered for TPT based on individualized risk assessments and sound clinical justification. 3. Other At-Risk Populations: Individuals initiating anti-TNF treatment, receiving dialysis, preparing for organ or hematological transplantation, or with silicosis should be systematically tested and treated for LTBI. Systematic LTBI testing and treatment may also be considered for prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from high TB burden countries, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. Systematic LTBI testing and treatment are not recommended for people with diabetes, those who engage in harmful alcohol use, tobacco smokers, or underweight individuals unless they belong to other high-risk groups. Algorithms to Rule Out Active TB Disease Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those without symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have active TB and should be offered TPT, regardless of their ART status. Individuals with any of these symptoms should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. If active TB is excluded, they should be offered TPT. Chest radiography may be used to rule out active TB in people living with HIV on ART, and TPT should be provided to those with no abnormal radiographic findings. Infants and children living with HIV who exhibit poor weight gain, fever, or cough, or have a history of contact with a TB patient, should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. If active TB is excluded, they should be offered TPT regardless of age. Testing for LTBI Either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) can be used to test for LTBI. TB Preventive Treatment Options Recommended regimens for LTBI treatment include 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid, a 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. Alternatives include a 1-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or 4 months of daily rifampicin alone. In high TB transmission settings, adults and adolescents living with HIV with unknown or positive LTBI test results and no active TB should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT), regardless of ART status, immunosuppression level, previous TB treatment, or pregnancy. Key Considerations for Implementation National programs should aim for universal TPT coverage among PLHIV and household contacts of TB patients under 5 years of age. Systematic screening for TB disease should be integrated with TPT services for at-risk populations. National policies should be updated to align with the latest global guidelines, and situational assessments should be conducted to identify target populations and address gaps in resources and health system capacity. Conclusion Tuberculosis remains the leading infectious killer worldwide. TPT is a critical intervention that preserves health, reduces deaths and transmission, and prevents catastrophic costs for families.
